A1.justification: Both readable 11-page PDFs describe the same STAGE work, with corresponding sections, equations, six figures and two tables. Neither contains an appendix or embedded supplement; both reference supplementary metric details not included in the supplied PDFs.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark comparisons and ablations in Table 1, human-preference results in Table 2, and generated examples in Figures 4–6.

after.justification: v2 retains the original benchmark, ablation, human-preference and qualitative generation results in Tables 1–2 and Figures 4–6.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same STEP2 model, multi-shot memory pack, dual-encoding strategy, supervised and preference-alignment training, and director/refiner video-generation workflow.

E1.justification: Both use the same ConStoryBoard and ConStoryBoard-HP data derived from Condensed Movies for storyboard-conditioned multi-shot generation. No dataset, task, domain or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain the same five comparators: CineTrans, IC-LoRA + WanX, StoryDiffusion + WanX, VideoGen-of-Thought and MovieAgent. Their participation in the quantitative, qualitative and human comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: The 100K training/1K testing pairs, 100K supervised plus 20K preference-training iterations, evaluation metrics and procedures are unchanged. Both human studies specify 20 samples and 25 volunteers per experiment.

E4.justification: Section 5.4, Table 1 and Figure 5 retain the same removals of the memory pack, dual encoding and two-stage training. Section 5.5 and Figure 6 retain the same nine-shot generation example.

E5.justification: Both report the same point-score and preference-percentage reporting practices. Neither supplies repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–2 match, as do the qualitative examples and findings in Figures 4–6. For example, STAGE's TVS remains 0.2732 and its shot-consistency preference remains 72.8%.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(10), including memory compression, flow matching, preference optimization and workflow definitions, are unchanged. No mathematical assumption, derivation or proof is added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about controllable generation, cross-shot coherence, cinematic transitions and ConStoryBoard. The added code-access sentence does not change a scientific claim.

C2.justification: The interpretations of comparisons and ablations are identical. Both retain the limitation that off-the-shelf video infilling can introduce temporal inconsistencies and the proposed future integration into an end-to-end backbone.

D1.justification: v2 adds 'Our code will be available at this url' at the abstract's end on page 2, linked to a specific GitHub repository; v1 has no code pointer. This adds prospective access information without establishing that code is released. Implementation details and the dataset-release promise are unchanged.

R1.justification: Both contain the same 60 cited works and identical related-work positioning. Differences in reference back-reference page numbers reflect pagination, not changed citations.

P1.justification: The substantive prose and section sequence are unchanged. v2 adds the short code-availability sentence and updates the arXiv version/date text, without broader rewriting or narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Text and equations reflow across columns and pages, and Table 2 moves from page 7 to page 8. All six figures, both table structures and their captions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 adds a concrete repository pointer for the promised code release, modestly improving access documentation. The method, evidence, conclusions and limitations are unchanged, and the PDFs do not establish actual code availability. The benefit is therefore limited to documentation; the layout changes have no material effect on scientific quality.
